h1: Rehydrating dry yeast properly before you pitch it
title: Rehydrating Dry Yeast Before You Pitch | Craft Beer School
desc: How to rehydrate dry brewing yeast properly: water temperature, ratio, timing, tempering and when direct pitching is fine.
teaser: Sprinkling dry yeast on wort works. Rehydrating it first works better. It takes fifteen minutes.
standfirst: Dry yeast is the easiest, most reliable yeast for Indian homebrewers. How you wake it up affects how many cells survive to do the work. Here is the simple method and the mistakes to avoid.
sections:
Dry yeast is alive but dormant, with almost all its water removed. When it hits liquid, the cell walls have to rebuild fast. In plain water at the right temperature, that happens smoothly. Dropped straight onto sugary wort, the cells face a strong osmotic pull while still fragile. Some of them do not survive.

Many beers ferment fine with direct pitching. Some yeast makers now say particular strains tolerate it. Rehydrating still gives more healthy cells for the same sachet, which means a quicker start and less stress on the yeast. Our guide to pitching yeast properly explains why cell count matters.

• Clean water: boiled and cooled tap water, or sealed packaged drinking water.
  • A sanitised jug or jar.
  • A thermometer.
  • Something sanitised to stir with.

Use about ten times the yeast's weight in water. For an 11 g sachet, that is around 110 ml. For a commercial brick, scale up accordingly.

1. Check the pack. Read the maker's rehydration temperature. Many brands sit somewhere between about 25 and 35 °C. Some differ, so follow the sachet.
  2. Bring the water to temperature in the sanitised jug.
  3. Sprinkle the yeast evenly on the surface. Do not dump it in a clump.
  4. Leave it for about 15 minutes without stirring.
  5. Stir gently into a creamy slurry and leave another 5 to 15 minutes, following the pack's total time.
  6. Temper it. If your wort is much cooler than the slurry, add a little wort to the jug a few times over ten minutes so the temperature gap is under about 10 °C before pitching.
  7. Pitch. Pour the slurry into the wort and stir or swirl.

• Water too hot. Above about 40 °C, yeast cells start to die. Check with a thermometer, not your finger.
  • Water too cold. Cold water during rehydration damages the cells too, as their membranes leak.
  • Rehydrating in wort. The point is to let cells recover in plain water first.
  • Leaving it too long. Do not leave rehydrated yeast sitting for hours before pitching. Have your wort ready first.
  • Temperature shock. Pouring 30 °C slurry into 15 °C lager wort is a jolt. Temper it.

Indian homebrewers usually have more trouble with heat than cold. Dry yeast survives transit far better than liquid yeast, but a sachet that sat on a sunny shop counter or in a hot delivery van has lost some of its strength. Buy from shops that keep yeast in the fridge and store it there at home. In summer, tap water left in the jug can sit well above the rehydration range, so check it.

If your tap water is chlorinated, boil and cool it, or use packaged drinking water. Our guide to the dry versus liquid yeast choice explains why dry yeast suits most Indian homebrewers in the first place.

One 11 g sachet is usually enough for 20 litres of an ordinary-strength ale. Stronger beers above about 1.060 and lagers need more cells. Many brewers use two sachets for a 20 litre lager or a big ale. Lagers ferment cold and slowly, so the extra yeast keeps the start quick and the flavour clean.

Unopened sachets keep well in the fridge until the best-before date printed on them, often a year or more from production. Keep them away from the freezer compartment and do not let them go through repeated warm and cold cycles. An opened sachet should be used that day, because the yeast starts taking up moisture from the air as soon as the seal is broken.

Write the purchase date on the pack and use the oldest first. If you buy yeast in bulk with friends, split it into sealed portions straight away rather than opening a brick each brew day.

Fermentation should start within roughly 12 to 24 hours for an ale at its normal temperature, often sooner. Look for bubbles, a layer of foam (krausen) and a falling gravity reading. If nothing happens after a day and a half, check the temperature first, then consider pitching fresh yeast. Our guide to yeast viability and vitality explains what a slow start can mean.
faqs: Do I have to rehydrate dry yeast?
No, but it usually gives more healthy cells and a quicker start. Some makers say certain strains handle direct pitching well.
What temperature should rehydration water be?
Follow the yeast pack. Many brands fall between about 25 and 35 °C. Never go above about 40 °C.
Can I rehydrate yeast in wort?
It is better to use plain water first, because sugary wort puts fragile cells under osmotic stress.
How long should I rehydrate dry yeast?
Usually about 15 to 30 minutes in total. Follow the pack and pitch soon afterwards.
